plain_english: Before you commit to anything, think about what comes before and what comes after. Then decide. Otherwise you'll start with excitement, ignore the consequences, and when they hit you, you'll quit in shame. "I want to win at the Olympics." Fine. But think about what that really means. If it's worth it, go for it. You'll have to follow strict rules. You'll have to diet. No treats. You'll have to train your body at set times whether you feel like it or not, in blazing heat and freezing cold. No cold water. Sometimes no wine at all. You basically have to hand your life over to your trainer like you would to a doctor. Then in the actual competition, you might get thrown in a ditch, dislocate your arm, twist your ankle, swallow tons of dust, get beaten for screwing up, and lose anyway. Add all that up. If you still want to do it, then go fight.
original_excerpt: In every affair consider what precedes and what follows, and then undertake it. Otherwise you will begin with spirit, indeed, careless of the consequences, and when these are developed, you will shamefully desist. "I would conquer at the Olympic Games." But consider what precedes and what follows, and then, if it be for your advantage, engage in the affair. You must conform to rules, submit to a diet, refrain from dainties; exercise your body, whether you choose it or not, at a stated hour, in heat and cold; you must drink no cold water, and sometimes no wine—in a word, you must give yourself up to your trainer as to a physician. Then, in the combat, you may be thrown into a ditch, dislocate your arm, turn your ankle, swallow an abundance of dust, receive stripes [for negligence], and, after all, lose the victory. When you have reckoned up all this, if your inclination still holds, set about the combat.

plain_english: If you don't watch out, you'll act like children at play. Kids see wrestlers and decide they're wrestlers. They see gladiators and become gladiators. They hear a trumpet and start playing trumpet. They watch a play and become actors. That's exactly what you'll do. One day you're a wrestler, the next a gladiator. Today a philosopher, tomorrow a public speaker. But you're never serious about any of it. Like a monkey, you copy whatever catches your eye. You get excited about something new, then lose interest as soon as the novelty wears off. You never think anything through. You never examine the whole picture or test whether it's right for you. You just jump in carelessly with half-hearted enthusiasm.
original_excerpt: Otherwise, take notice, you will behave like children who sometimes play wrestlers, sometimes gladiators, sometimes blow a trumpet, and sometimes act a tragedy, when they happen to have seen and admired these shows. Thus you too will be at one time a wrestler, and another a gladiator; now a philosopher, now an orator; but nothing in earnest. Like an ape you mimic all you see, and one thing after another is sure to please you, but is out of favor as soon as it becomes familiar. For you have never entered upon anything considerately; nor after having surveyed and tested the whole matter, but carelessly, and with a halfway zeal.

plain_english: Some people hear a philosopher speak—someone like Euphrates (though really, who can speak like him?)—and they think, "I want to be a philosopher too." Hold on. First, figure out what this actually involves. And be honest about what you can handle. If you wanted to be a wrestler, you'd check your shoulders, your back, your thighs. Different people are built for different things. Do you think you can keep living exactly like you do now and be a philosopher? Keep eating, drinking, getting angry, and complaining the way you always have? You'll need to stay alert. You'll need to work hard. You'll have to control certain desires. You'll have to leave some friends behind. Your servant will look down on you. People you meet will laugh at you. You'll lose out to others in everything—jobs, honors, court cases.
original_excerpt: Thus some, when they have seen a philosopher and heard a man speaking like Euphrates[3]—though, indeed, who can speak like him?—have a mind to be philosophers, too. Consider first, man, what the matter is, and what your own nature is able to bear. If you would be a wrestler, consider your shoulders, your back, your thighs; for different persons are made for different things. Do you think that you can act as you do and be a philosopher, that you can eat, drink, be angry, be discontented, as you are now? You must watch, you must labor, you must get the better of certain appetites, must quit your acquaintances, be despised by your servant, be laughed at by those you meet; come off worse than others in everything—in offices, in honors, before tribunals.

plain_english: After you've thought through all of this, then make your choice—if you want to give up those things to buy peace of mind, freedom, and calm. If not, don't bother. Don't be like children who play philosopher one day, businessman the next, then speaker, then government official. You can't have it both ways. You must be one person, either good or bad. Either work on your own thinking or chase external things. Focus on what's within you or what's outside you. Be either a philosopher or just another person in the crowd.
original_excerpt: When you have fully considered all these things, approach, if you please—that is, if, by parting with them, you have a mind to purchase serenity, freedom, and tranquillity. If not, do not come hither; do not, like children, be now a philosopher, then a publican, then an orator, and then one of Caesar's officers. These things are not consistent. You must be one man, either good or bad. You must cultivate either your own reason or else externals; apply yourself either to things within or without you—that is, be either a philosopher or one of the mob.
